'''Marija Drndic''' (born November 2, 1971) is the Fay R. and Eugene L. Langberg Professor of Physics at the [[University of Pennsylvania]]. She works on [[two-dimensional materials]] and novel spectroscopic techniques.

== Early life and education ==
Drndic studied physics and mathematics at [[Harvard University]] and spent a year at the [[University of Cambridge]] in the Semiconductor Physics Group.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.physics.upenn.edu/people/standing-faculty/marija-drndic|title=Marija Drndic {{!}} Department of Physics and Astronomy|website=www.physics.upenn.edu|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref> At [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]] Drndic worked on quantum transport of coupled gases with [[Michael Pepper]].<ref name=":0" /> At [[Harvard University]] she was a member of [[Phi Beta Kappa]] and graduated [[summa cum laude]]. Drndic was awarded a [[Clare Boothe Luce|Clare Booth Luce]] Fellowship, the Harold T. White Prize for Excellence in Teaching and the Robbins Prize from [[Harvard University]]. She remained there for her doctoral studies, working with [[Robert Westervelt]] on microelectromagnets for cold-atom experiments. She before joining the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as a Pappalardo Fellow.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://web.mit.edu/physics/research/pappalardo/fellows.html#former|title=MIT Department of Physics|website=web.mit.edu|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref> As a postdoctoral researcher Drndic worked on electron transport in [[cadmium selenide]] nanocrystals. She worked alongside [[Marc A. Kastner]] and [[Moungi Bawendi]] on novel spectroscopies.<ref name=":0" />

== Research and career ==
In 2003 Drndic joined the [[University of Pennsylvania]]. She was awarded an [[American Chemical Society]] Petroleum Research Fund Award in 2004, and has since been supported by the [[National Science Foundation]], [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] and [[DARPA]]. In 2005 Drndic was awarded a [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pennmedicine.org/news/news-releases/2005/june/two-penn-school-of-medicine|title=Two Penn School of Medicine Professors Honored at White House for Research and Community Service – PR News|website=www.pennmedicine.org|language=en-US|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref>

Her work considers low-dimensional materials including nanowires, nanocrystals and biomaterials.<ref name=":0" /> Drndic uses electron beams to image and shape materials.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mrs-serbia.org.rs/index.php/symposium-f-renowned-scientists-from-ex-yugoslavia/2d-materials-nanosculpting-and-bioelectronics-applications|title=Materials Research Society of Serbia - Marija Drndic, 2D Materials Nanosculpting and Bioelectronics Applications|website=www.mrs-serbia.org.rs|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref> In particular, Drndic works on [[Two-dimensional materials|two-dimensional]] [[nanopore]]s, which are nanoscale size holes that can be used to detect single molecules. They are typically used for biomolecular analysis, but were unable to sequence [[DNA]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Drndić|first=Marija|date=2014|title=Sequencing with graphene pores|journal=Nature Nanotechnology|volume=9|issue=10|pages=743|doi=10.1038/nnano.2014.232|pmid=25286264|bibcode=2014NatNa...9..743D |issn=1748-3387|doi-access=free}}</ref> Drndic demonstrated it is possible to use light to control the shape of [[nanopore]]s, indicating it may be possible to fabricate them using light.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/penn-researchers-control-size-2-d-nanopores-light|title=Penn Researchers Control the Size of 2-D Nanopores With Light|website=Penn Today|date=16 March 2017 |language=en|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref> By removing individual atoms from the [[nanopore]]s using [[Ion-beam sculpting|ion beams]], Drndic demonstrated that the nanopores can also be used in water desalination.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://penntoday.upenn.edu/spotlights/creating-atomic-water-filters|title=Creating atomic water filters|website=Penn Today|date=15 March 2018 |language=en|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref> She has shown that [[nanopore]]s can be integrated with [[field-effect transistor]]s to sense nearby ionic and electrical currents.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.carbonhagen.com/abstracts-1/invited-2019/marijadrndiconceuponatimetherewasa2dnanopore|title=Marija Drndic: Once upon a time, there was a 2D nanopore - Carbonhagen2019|website=www.carbonhagen.com|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref> They can also provide information on the physical and chemical properties of [[biomolecule]]s including [[DNA]] and [[protein]]s.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/beyond-graphene-two-penn-projects-will-look-biological-applications-new-2-d-materials|title=Two Penn Projects Will Look at Biological Applications of New 2-D Materials|website=Penn Today|date=23 September 2015 |language=en|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/penn-researchers-use-nanoscopic-pores-investigate-protein-structure|title=Penn Researchers Use Nanoscopic Pores to Investigate Protein Structure|website=Penn Today|date=17 August 2015 |language=en|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref>

=== Selected publications ===
Her publications include;

* {{Cite journal|title=DNA translocation through graphene nanopores|last=Drndic|first=Marija|date=2010|journal=Nano Letters|volume=10|issue=8|pages=2915–2921|doi=10.1021/nl101046t|pmid=20698604|bibcode=2010NanoL..10.2915M }}
* {{Cite journal|title=Rapid electronic detection of probe-specific microRNAs using thin nanopore sensors|last=Drndic|first=Marija|date=2010|journal=Nature Nanotechnology|volume=5|issue=11|pages=807–814|doi=10.1038/nnano.2010.202|pmid=20972437|bibcode=2010NatNa...5..807W }}
* {{Cite journal|title=Electron beam nanosculpting of suspended graphene sheets|last=Drndic|first=Marija|date=2008|journal=Applied Physics Letters|volume=93|issue=11|article-number=113107|doi=10.1063/1.2980518|arxiv=0808.2974 |bibcode=2008ApPhL..93k3107F |s2cid=119272690|url=https://repository.upenn.edu/physics_papers/91|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200531192858/https://repository.upenn.edu/physics_papers/91/|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 31, 2020}}

Drndic holds several patents for electronic devices and thin film structures.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.justia.com/inventor/marija-drndic|title=Marija Drndic Inventions, Patents and Patent Applications - Justia Patents Search|website=patents.justia.com|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref>
